```{r}
library(pdecompR)
library(Matrix)
```

## Element loops without loops

Assembly computes, for every element $T$ and every pair of local basis
functions,

$$
A^T_{ij} = \sum_q w_q \det B_T \left[ c\,\phi_i\phi_j + \phi_i\,(b\cdot\nabla\phi_j)
+ \nabla\phi_i^\top D\,\nabla\phi_j \right](\hat x_q),
$$

with $i$ the test index (row) and $j$ the trial index (column). pdecompR
vectorizes over elements: the loops run over quadrature points and the
$3\times3$ (or $6\times6$) local indices, while each operation acts on a
vector of length $m$ (the number of elements). The local matrices are then
summed into a global sparse matrix through triplets
$(I, J, A^T_{ij})$, which `Matrix::sparseMatrix()` accumulates into the
compressed column format.

```{r}
V <- fe_space(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 16))
K <- assemble_matrix(V, "stiffness")
M <- assemble_matrix(V, "mass")
C <- assemble_matrix(V, "advection", c(1, 0))
class(K); dim(K); nnzero(K)
```

The structure reflects the mesh connectivity:

```{r}
image(K[1:60, 1:60], main = "stiffness pattern (first 60 dofs)")
```

## Properties worth checking

```{r}
max(abs(K %*% rep(1, V$ndof)))   # constants are in the kernel of K
sum(M)                           # 1' M 1 is the area
isSymmetric(K); isSymmetric(M)
range(eigen(as.matrix(M), only.values = TRUE)$values)
```

The stiffness matrix with Dirichlet rows and columns removed is symmetric
positive definite; the advection matrix is not symmetric.

## Tensor coefficients

Anisotropic diffusion uses a symmetric tensor
`tensor_coefficient(xx, xy, yy)`, whose entries are numbers or functions of
`(x, y)`. Positive definiteness is checked at every quadrature point.

```{r}
D <- tensor_coefficient(xx = 1, xy = 0.3, yy = function(x, y) 0.2 + x)
D
sa <- solve_pde(elliptic_problem(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 16), diffusion = D, source = 1,
                                 bcs = dirichlet_bc(0)))
range(sa$u$values)
```

## Load vectors and boundary terms

```{r}
b <- assemble_vector(V, function(x, y) x * y)
sum(b)                                            # int x y = 1/4
sum(assemble_boundary_vector(V, 1, "left"))       # length of the left edge
```

## Projection between meshes

`l2_project(f, space)` computes the $L^2$ projection: the function in the
space with the same integrals against every basis function. Unlike
interpolation it preserves the integral of `f`. For a finite-element
function on an unrelated mesh, the load integrals are computed exactly on
the overlay (common refinement) of the two meshes, so the integral over the
whole domain is preserved up to rounding. Integrals over single elements
or groups of elements are not preserved in general; that would need a
discontinuous space. The two meshes must cover the same domain, otherwise
the projection is rejected. `errornorm()` uses the same overlay to compare
solutions on unrelated meshes.

```{r}
a <- interpolate(function(x, y) sin(5 * x) * y, fe_space(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 12)))
W <- fe_space(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 5, pattern = "left"))
pr <- l2_project(a, W); it <- interpolate(a, W)
c(source = sum(assemble_vector(a$space, 1) * a$values),
  projection = sum(assemble_vector(W, 1) * pr$values),
  interpolation = sum(assemble_vector(W, 1) * it$values))
```

## Invariance under renumbering

Assembly does not depend on the order of nodes: renumbering the nodes
permutes the matrix.

```{r}
m <- pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 4)
perm <- sample(nrow(m$nodes)); inv <- order(perm)
m2 <- pde_mesh(m$nodes[perm, ], matrix(inv[m$triangles], ncol = 3))
K1 <- as.matrix(assemble_matrix(fe_space(m), "stiffness"))
K2 <- as.matrix(assemble_matrix(fe_space(m2), "stiffness"))
max(abs(K2 - K1[perm, perm]))
```

## Linear solvers

`solve_linear_system()` chooses sparse Cholesky for symmetric matrices (with
a fallback to sparse LU when the matrix is not positive definite) and sparse
LU otherwise. Preconditioned conjugate gradients, BiCGSTAB and restarted
GMRES are also available.

```{r}
A <- K + M
rhs <- assemble_vector(V, 1)
for (m in c("auto", "lu", "cg", "bicgstab", "gmres")) {
  s <- solve_linear_system(A, rhs, method = m, tol = 1e-12)
  cat(sprintf("%-8s %-9s iterations %4s  relative residual %.2e\n", m, s$info$method,
              s$info$iterations, s$info$relative_residual))
}
```

Every solve reports a status, the residual and its relative size, the
iteration count, the matrix size and the number of nonzeros. Iterative
methods report `"not converged"` instead of returning silently:

```{r}
solve_linear_system(A, rhs, method = "cg", maxit = 3)$info$status
```

For repeated solves with the same matrix (time stepping), `linear_solver()`
factors once and returns a reusable `solve()` function. A matrix right-hand
side solves several systems with one factorization.

Direct solves first scale the matrix symmetrically by
$D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}$ with $D = |\mathrm{diag}(A)|$, which removes the
effect of badly scaled coefficients on the pivoting and on the residual
test.

### Preconditioners and multigrid

The Krylov methods take `preconditioner = "jacobi"` (the default),
`"ssor"`, `"none"`, or a function `function(r)` that applies an
approximate inverse. On a hierarchy of nested meshes,
`multigrid_preconditioner()` builds a geometric multigrid V-cycle: exact P1
prolongation from the refinement record, Galerkin coarse operators,
symmetric Gauss-Seidel smoothing and a direct solve on the coarsest mesh.
Its iteration count stays bounded under refinement, while Jacobi's grows
like $h^{-1}$:

```{r}
meshes <- list(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 4))
for (k in 1:4) meshes[[k + 1]] <- refine_uniform(meshes[[k]])
p <- poisson_problem(meshes[[5]], source = 1, boundary = dirichlet_bc(0))
its <- sapply(list(jacobi = "jacobi", ssor = "ssor", multigrid = multigrid_preconditioner(meshes)),
              function(pc) solve_pde(p, method = "cg", preconditioner = pc)$diagnostics$solver$iterations)
its
```

The multigrid preconditioner works for P1 problems on meshes produced by
`refine_uniform()` or `refine_mesh()`.

Without a mesh hierarchy, or for P2 spaces, `amg_preconditioner()` builds
the hierarchy from the matrix by smoothed aggregation. On an unstructured
L-shaped mesh with P2 elements its iteration count barely moves while
Jacobi's doubles with each halving of `h` (at `h = 0.025`, about 130,000
unknowns, Jacobi CG reaches its iteration limit while AMG needs 37
iterations):

```{r}
L <- pde_domain("polygon", vertices = cbind(c(0, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0), c(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2)))
sapply(c(0.1, 0.05), function(h) {
  p <- poisson_problem(pde_mesh_polygon(L, h = h), source = 1, boundary = dirichlet_bc(0), degree = 2)
  c(h = h, jacobi = solve_pde(p, method = "cg")$diagnostics$solver$iterations,
    amg = solve_pde(p, method = "cg", preconditioner = amg_preconditioner())$diagnostics$solver$iterations)
})
```

In two dimensions the sparse Cholesky factorization remains faster than AMG
preconditioned CG at every size measured (0.53 s against 0.82 s for 66,000
P2 unknowns on the unit square, with similar peak memory), so the direct
solver stays the default. AMG is the choice among the iterative methods:
far fewer iterations than Jacobi or SSOR, and it applies where geometric
multigrid cannot (P2 spaces, unstructured meshes without a refinement
hierarchy).

## Cost

Assembly is linear in the number of elements, and so is the memory of the
sparse matrices. The supernodal Cholesky factorization of two-dimensional
finite-element matrices costs roughly $O(N^{1.5})$ operations with fill
reducing orderings, which keeps meshes with $10^5$ to $10^6$ unknowns
practical on a workstation.

```{r}
for (n in c(16, 32, 64)) {
  mesh <- pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = n)
  t <- system.time(s <- solve_pde(poisson_problem(mesh, source = 1, boundary = dirichlet_bc(0))))
  cat(sprintf("n = %3d  dofs = %6d  assembly %.2fs  solve %.2fs\n", n, s$space$ndof,
              s$diagnostics$assembly_time, s$diagnostics$solve_time))
}
```

Where coefficients change every time step or Newton iteration, the matrix
is reassembled on a fixed sparsity pattern: the map from element entries to
the nonzeros is computed once, and each reassembly is one sparse
matrix-vector product, about twelve times faster than building the matrix
from triplets. The element integrals themselves then dominate (about 80
percent of a reassembly for P1 on a 128 by 128 mesh), so the end-to-end
gain is modest: 7 percent for a heat problem with time-dependent diffusion
and 4 percent for a quasilinear Newton solve.

`benchmarks/protocol.R` in the source repository runs each case in a fresh
R process under `/usr/bin/time` for the true peak memory, repeats it after
a warm-up run and reports the median with the range, and compares P1, P2
and AMG solves at a fixed error. On the unit square P2 reaches an L2 error
of `1e-5` with 4,225 unknowns, where P1 needs more than 66,000.
